Messages.Author: Ventru...@hotmail.com
Messages.Body:
It came to me the other day that people are possibly losing the feeling of
this game. While I will admit that game mechanics are very important (working
out the best deck and winning - obviously) it does seem as though peoiple
flow through games without a cross thought as to what it's all about.

Now I'm not berating anyone for this, I justr think that the games have a
danger of becoming too faceless (ie combat - card after card churned out
without anyone thinking 'Hey, I just called some carrion crows, that's cool!'
or at least picturing it in their heads.)

I personally love this game and I'm sure you all do too. Sometimes though,
it's in danger of falling into the 4 suit variety of games.

What do people think?

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Ventru...@hotmail.com wrote:
>
> It came to me the other day that people are possibly losing the feeling of
> this game. While I will admit that game mechanics are very important
> (working out the best deck and winning - obviously) it does seem as though

> people flow through games without a cross thought as to what it's all
> about.

Well, you have to realize that this game has a very complex strategy
element. It's that complexity which attracts people like me to this
game. I have no interest in playing the role-playing game, and while
I'm mildly interested in the vampire genre (big Buffy fan!), that's not
the driving force behind my interest in this game.

If you personally want to play the game saying "hey, neat" and "cool"
every time anyone plays a card, feel free. I, on the other hand, prefer
to play on a more abstract level. When someone plays Deflection or
Govern the Unaligned, I hardly ever think about what the card means in
non-game terms. (For example, I just recently for the first time
noticed the big glowing hand on GtU.)

When you play Risk, do you get upset when people don't say "Hmm... I'm
invading Kamchatka. Rejoice, Kamchatkans! I have liberated you from
your oppressors!" I think most people play Risk by moving their little
pieces around and rolling a bunch of dice. Someone might joke around
and say the above, but the game is not being taken that seriously.

> Now I'm not berating anyone for this, I just think that the games have a

> danger of becoming too faceless (ie combat - card after card churned out
> without anyone thinking 'Hey, I just called some carrion crows, that's
> cool!' or at least picturing it in their heads.)

If you want to play a game where this is the expected norm, maybe you
should play the RPG instead. In an RPG, there are no "victory
conditions." People aren't playing to win; they're trying to accurately
portray their characters and have fun doing in. In a CCG, there are
victory conditions, and people playing the CCG should be playing to win.

> I personally love this game and I'm sure you all do too. Sometimes though,
> it's in danger of falling into the 4 suit variety of games.

Both VTES and, say, Bridge have large strategy elements. VTES has a lot
more different cards, and a lot more rules. It's intriguing to me that
I can get about as much enjoyment out of a game of VTES as a few rounds
of Bridge. Again, it sounds like you want to turn every game of VTES
into a role-playing session. Don't get upset when you encounter other
people who are playing the card game for what it is.

James
--
James Hamblin
ham...@math.wisc.edu

Let me tell you something, you can't win."

i think you'll find that a lot of the people on this group couldn't give a
rat's arse about the story/real world aspects of the game. As Rob Treasure
once memorably commented to me, the pictures on the cards could be piles of
dog poo for all he cares - it is the GAME and its mechanics, not the
background or connection to vampires, which interests him. Also, it is often
quite hard to picture what a card is "really" doing - DotS, DI, SR, ToR3,
ToGP, Political Flux are ones that spring to mind as difficult to provide a
real-world story for. David Zopf keeps saying [and i keep agreeing with him]
that the game is an abstract and high-level representation of an Endless
Conflict between indestructible ancients and it's not to be judged in terms
of
linkage [for example] to the frippery concerns and frank misconceptions of
the
ancillae as represented in the RPG.

i agree that this would be a fine game even if it was about the endless
conflict between piles of dog-poo but i also sympathise with the gist of
your
post which i take to be that it's fun to think about the doings of your
minions too. This idea informs the building of the decks we use for
home-play.
No doubt many people will criticise me for keeping my home play-group in the
dark with regard to competitive jyhad but i honestly did try to influence
them
in that direction and i failed - they like to play a card-based RPG,
essentially, and they get bored by weird technical combos and
excessively-fast
games. i like playing both ways, me - hare/hounds sorta thing, but it's
true!

My advice would be to accept the fact that Caine's house hath many mansions
and to find the one that is decorated most closely to your taste. If you
like
the role-playing aspect best then you can come round to my house and play in
our sub-competitive games [or start a group of your own]; if you like the
hard-core competitive aspect then nowanights there are x million tourneys
for
you to enter. All to the good, i say.

artistic allegory to suggest simply that the vampire has called on his
training/discipline/blood resources or whatever to make some particularly
strong punches/swipes in this combat. The "Torn Signpost" is a sign or
symbol of what transpired, not the cause of it.

Other cards do something like the same thing: describe an effect rather
than a literal cause. "The Death of My Conscience"? Com'on! It wasn't
anyone's conscience that was holding 'em back from destroying their enemies.
"Blood Agony" - the user doesn't suffer the blood agony, it's the victim.
Same with "Weakness". "Sacrament of Carnage" - I doubt the vampire first
performs a rite of any kind and then are gifted with the boon of causing
ranged damage. Like Torn Signpost, it's just a fanciful way of describing
the aftermath.

> persuades me that there's a great story there, if I only knew it.

Agreed. And it's one of the things I've grown to like about the game.
Magic, too. Not everything has to be so literal.

Like imagining you are playing with Dog Poo? (Damn, I love that one

> When someone plays Deflection or

The name of the card is referring to the superior power I guess. Influencing
younger vampires, just like we are doing as ancient Methuselahs.

Torn Signpost is a bit weird as it is an actual object, which seems to have
little to do with its effect. I guess stronger vampires could rip a signpost
apart easily, but that doesn't make much sense having it as a name for a
card. Also, if the signpost is supposed to represent an improvised weapon,
then it seems strange that the card represents only an increase in hand
damage and is not a melee weapon. (I always thought a pool cue would make a
nice long-reach stake in a pinch).

Sacrament of Carnage is referring to one of the religious tenets of the
Sabbat I think... but from the old books. I don't remember this one and
don't have my books handy, but there are a lot of minor religious rites, and
this could represent one (that does not explain why it is a Potence card
though).

'Blood Agony' and 'Weakness' are both levels of Quietus in the RPG, similar
to 'Earth Meld' or 'Wolf Claws' for Protean.

One discipline is conspicuously absent from the CCG, the second level of
Dominate, 'Forgetful Mind'. The strange thing is that it seems like a power
that is rife with applications in Jyhad. I suppose making Dominate even MORE
powerful than it already is might be unnecessary.

> > Now I'm not berating anyone for this, I just think that the games have a
> > danger of becoming too faceless (ie combat - card after card churned out
> > without anyone thinking 'Hey, I just called some carrion crows, that's
> > cool!' or at least picturing it in their heads.)

While it doesn't make any difference in the end whether you play the theme
or not, I think for me personally it enhances the fun imagining the
struggles of ancient vampires and their minions. I totally play the game on
two levels... one as a complex strategy game, and two as a huge fan of the
'World of Darkness'.

For example, regardless of their effectiveness, I rarely if ever play
Malkavian decks. I think this comes down to just how much I hated players
who had Malkavian characters in the LARP in Detroit a few years back. I just
don't like the 'theme' of Malks enough to play with them.

On the other hand, I will often play with clans that I have enjoyed in the
RPG or whose concept I like even if they are considered crap. I love
Assamites and Setites and will play Jyhad with them even if they are nearly
impossible to win with in their present form.

I think it was in the original Jyhad reference-guide-book-thingee where they
were discussing how the cards were developed. The designer mentioned that
when they originally playtested the cards they used images that had no
association at all with the card name or function. For example, I think
Ulugh Beg was a picture of a rocking horse (with all the text associated
with UB). This was so they could have SOMETHING for visual reference before
they had to actually print the final version of the cards. After playing
many test games, the rocking horse became associated with the card itself.

> If you want to play a game where this is the expected norm, maybe you
> should play the RPG instead. In an RPG, there are no "victory
> conditions." People aren't playing to win; they're trying to accurately
> portray their characters and have fun doing in. In a CCG, there are
> victory conditions, and people playing the CCG should be playing to win.

Actually, the very WORST kinds of role-players DO try to win, which is
absurd. It's one of the aspects of RPG's that turn me off.

> > I personally love this game and I'm sure you all do too. Sometimes
though,
> > it's in danger of falling into the 4 suit variety of games.

I agree completely. If only to inject some humour into games like this, I
like to elaborate on actions with a bit of silly improvisation. Anson
doesn't just go to torpor, he 'dives into the ground to recover from mortal
wounds'. Sela doesn't just play 'Torn Signpost', she 'rips a sign out of the
ground in seething rage'. Not that my fiction in the Brujah-Antitribu
newsletters are worthy of special attention, but I came up with the 'plots'
based on pulling a few cards out and pasting them into something resembling
a narrative.

I've even been trying to leave about 10 % of each deck for cards that are
just fun corner case cards. This makes the decks less effective but often a
hell of a lot more fun. Sometimes cards that seem useless will pop out of
nowhere and surprise everyone. In fact, this was always something I
appreciated back when we played with 4CL... there was a lot less
predictability in any deck we saw. There was no such thing as IG combat
decks, there were no decks with 40 Weather Controls in them. Decks were a
lot more random/unfocused than they are now and somehow this only added to
our enjoyment of them.

Whatever the game is about, it's supposed to be fun, and fuck it if we all
take it too seriously.

Oh well... there's my $0.02 CDN for you. I'm going to go make an Aggravated
Dog Poo deck now.

Cheers,
WES

But its a rare day that I state it so eloquently... (I'll save
Ventrue Harpy my typical anti-RPG rant) My main concern is when role
players attempt to make a card game into a variant method of playing
their RPG. Good card games won't do that at all well, and bad ones
wouldn't do it nearly well enough to satisfy any RPGer. I'm amazed
most people don't recognize that. Especially tabletop roleplayers and
LARPers. If there was ever a group whom I would think would avoid
trying to jam the square peg in the round hole, its them. I think what
they want (a more exacting mirror of VTM rules mechanics and cannon)
is really unattainable, and my typically curt, often rude responses
derive from their attempts to (fruitlessly) twist an exceptionally
good card game to and end that is really unattainable. Its unlikely
that you'll ever find a CCG that is at all capable of replacing an
RPG, and why in the world would a RPGer even want to try???

I think its best to leave the mechanics of the game as they are,
expand them where is prudent, and use the World of Darkness as the
thematic hook. It is an interesting one, after all.

Hrmmm.... You know what? ......Naah, stick with WoD.

I sympathize too, but I really think that this is more a concern to be
raised among peers in each person's play group, and is not a general
shortcoming of the game. If anything, the game allows almost too much
latitude for a whole spectrum of fun; tactical, colllecting, building
decks, competitive tournaments, and creative extrapolation like
'storytelling card games' (writing a fictional story based on
documented VTES game results). I suppose my point is that tactics,
deckbuilding and (to a lesser extent) tournaments are more often
ranked higher than the others in most players esteem. (and rightly so
for a card game)

>This idea informs the building of the decks we use for
>home-play.
>No doubt many people will criticise me for keeping my home play-group in the
>dark with regard to competitive jyhad but i honestly did try to influence
>them
>in that direction and i failed - they like to play a card-based RPG,
>essentially, and they get bored by weird technical combos and
>excessively-fast
>games. i like playing both ways, me - hare/hounds sorta thing, but it's

Happy Families comes closest to allowing for a card based RPG to
happen, but I think that your home-play group isn't looking so hard
for as tight a following to VTM cannon as what most VTM players ask
for. I agree with you and Ventrue Harpy, but I think what you are
really striving to create is not really a card based RPG so much as it
is an environment that is structured for even diverse play. Every
group attains this in some way, or stagnates and dies... In Boston
and Charlotte, I've tried to encourage people to be aware of what
intensity of deck their peers are playing so that the games can be
soemwhat evenly matched.
Players always come to the (non-tournament) table with objectives
different that just "gain VP", and this game delivers like no other in
allowing for those alternative objectives. All thats really needed is
for other players to be informed about what your goals are with a
deck, and maybe wriggle a little bit to accomodate... Happy Families
is great in that it sets a staged limitation that allows for more
balanced play among the clans. Most of us haven't evolved that level
of structure, but we get along ;-)

Regards,
R. David Zopf

Kevin wrote:
>>The V:TES version of the card says
the vampire may use +2 hand damage "as a strike" for the remainder of

Keep in mind that the pertinent part of the original Jyhad version (which was
printed before the VTES version) of TS says:

"Vampire does 2 hand damage for the remainder of combat."

What does this mean? It is unclear--they apparently didn't think to hard about
it when the card was originally designed, and the wording is ambigious--could
be a "strike" kinda card, or it could just increase your hand damage. At some
point after this card had been printed, but before the VTES version came out,
it was rulled by the powers that be at the time that TS did nothing but give
you 2 or 3 hand damage for the remainder of combat. Then the card was reprinted
in VTES with more (different) ambigious text that seemed to run counter to the
original ruling/errata for the card, so more clarification was issued that was
very clear--the only effect that TS has is that it gives a vampire 2 or 3 hand
damage for the remainder of combat. As there are plenty of cards (like melee
weapons or Undead Strength) that are based on a minions hand damage, TS
increases the damage these do as well.

Yes, the card has a picture of a signpost on it. It could very well have a
picture of a vampire snapping something in half on it, and that would have
removed all confusion from this card. It also could have been called "Fists of
Severe, But Not Fatal, Injury", and again, no confusion. It is unfortunate that
someone decided to name this card "Torn Signpost", and that the artist who
interpreted the art (and probably had no idea what the card actually did, let
alone how the game worked...) drew a signpost, but that is neither here nor
there. TS does only one thing--it increases your hand damage to 2 or 3.

>>This would both make more sense and it would differentiate
it from other potence cards. There is the rare card from the first set
that you have to pay one to have basically the same effect, which
becomes almost useless,>>

Nope. Fists of Death (the rare card in question) gives you +1/+2 hand damage,
rather than 2 or 3 hand damage. Thus FoD stacks with itself, TS, or other Pot
cards (if you play 3 FoD at superior, you get 7 hand damage. If you play 3 TS
at superior, you still only have 3 hand damage. If you play a TS and a FoD
together at Superior, you have 5 hand damage for only 1 blood, as opposed to if
you got that 5 hand damage by playing 2 FoD instead--TS and FoD are
interlocking parts--you need both, not just one or the other).

>>there is undead strength which is virtually the same thing but less useful
since it only works once.>>

But it is a strike, and stacks with both FoD and TS--if you play with only one
of these cards, you do a maximum of 3 damage from a hand strike. If you play
with 2 of them, you max out at 5 damage from a hand strike (unless you stack
the FoD, but that costs a lot of blood). If you use all three, you max out a 7
hand damage from a hand strike.

>>Sure either of these can be stacked, but that hardly seems like much of a
difference.>>

The difference is very important in a combat deck that wants do be able to
reliably torporize folks without using Celerity. Yeah, if you are relying on
TS/Blur for all your damage, then TS and FoD are pretty much interchangeable,
with TS being mostly better, 'cause it doesn't cost anything. On the other
hand, if you are the Nosferatu, Lasombra, Giovanni, or any other non Cel based
clan, this isn't an option, thus you need the stackability provided by TS,
FoD,and US (and this is why POT only decks generally beat POT/cel decks--the
POT deck punches you the first time for 7, while the POT/cel deck hits for only
3 or 5 in the first strike, hoping to Blur...)
